title: 26 U.S. Code Section 41(b)(4) Startup Ventures
description: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4), pre-revenue startup ventures can claim the federal R&D credit on in-house research expenses before launching a product.
summary: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4), pre-revenue startup ventures can claim the federal R&D tax credit on in-house research expenses—wages, supplies, and computer or cloud costs—before launching a product, if their principal purpose is to use the research in a future trade or business. The waiver excludes contract research, and California conforms with in-state limits.

body.text: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4), pre-revenue startup ventures can claim the federal R&D tax credit on in-house research expenses—wages, supplies, and computer or cloud costs—before launching a product, if their principal purpose is to use the research in a future trade or business. The waiver excludes contract research, and California conforms with in-state limits.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4), Congress explicitly waives the traditional active "trade or business" requirement of Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41(b)(1) for in-house research expenses incurred by pre-revenue startup ventures. Provided that a taxpayer's principal purpose at the time the in-house research expenditures are paid or incurred is to use the results of the research in the active conduct of a future trade or business—either of the taxpayer itself under IRC § 41(b)(4)(A) or of one or more aggregated affiliates treated as a single taxpayer under IRC §§ 41(b)(4)(B) and 41(f)(1)—the startup may generate federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credits prior to commercial launch or revenue generation. This statutory exception resolves a longstanding structural conflict in federal tax accounting between the restrictive "carrying on" standard of IRC § 162(a) and the capital-intensive timelines of early-stage scientific, software, biotechnology, and hardware engineering.

While 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4) eliminates the pre-commercialization barrier for in-house research wages, supplies, and leased computer (cloud computing) expenses under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A), it does not extend to third-party contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3), nor does it relax the substantive requirements of the statutory Four-Part Test under IRC § 41(d) or the funded research exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H). Furthermore, recent federal and state legislative developments have reshaped how startups account for and calculate these benefits. At the federal level, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025) added 26 U.S.C. § 174A, restoring immediate expensing for domestic research or experimental (R&E) expenditures for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, and replacing the mandatory five-year domestic amortization regime that applied from 2022 through 2024 under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA, Pub. L. 115-97). At the state level, California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) §§ 23609 and 17052.12 conform to the federal § 41(b)(4) startup waiver while imposing strict in-state geographic sourcing rules and transitioning, for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, from the repealed Alternative Incremental Credit (AIC) to a modified California Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) featuring a 3% standard rate and a 1.3% startup rate.
Federal Statutory Architecture and Legislative History of Section 41(b)(4)

Understanding the statutory mechanics of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4) requires examining how the Internal Revenue Code classifies pre-operational business expenditures across four intersecting provisions: IRC §§ 162, 195, 174 (now paired with § 174A), and 41. Each provision establishes a distinct operational nexus threshold between an expenditure and the taxpayer's commercial enterprise, determining whether a pre-revenue venture's outlays are currently deductible, subject to mandatory capitalization, or eligible for dollar-for-dollar general business tax credits.
The Section 162 Active Business Barrier and Section 195 Capitalization

Under traditional federal income tax accounting, 26 U.S.C. § 162(a) allows a current-year deduction for all ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred during the taxable year in "carrying on any trade or business". In Commissioner v. Groetzinger, 480 U.S. 23 (1987) (decided February 24, 1987, opinion by Justice Blackmun), the U.S. Supreme Court noted that while the phrase "trade or business" appears across over 50 Internal Revenue Code sections, 800 subsections, and hundreds of regulations without a single universal statutory definition, satisfying IRC § 162(a) requires that a taxpayer be involved in the activity with "continuity and regularity" and that the taxpayer's primary purpose for engaging in the activity be for income or profit. While the Groetzinger Court rejected Justice Frankfurter's concurring gloss from Deputy v. Du Pont that holding oneself out to others as selling goods or services is an absolute prerequisite in all contexts (holding that a full-time gambler wagering solely for his own account was engaged in a trade or business), the Court reaffirmed the foundational principle of Higgins v. Commissioner, 312 U.S. 212 (1941), that passive investment management does not constitute a trade or business. Under established IRC § 162(a) jurisprudence, active conduct of a trade or business does not commence until an enterprise begins performing the ongoing revenue-generating operations for which it was organized.

Because pre-revenue startups are not yet "carrying on" an active commercial operation, their pre-opening and investigatory expenditures are barred from immediate deduction under IRC § 162(a). Instead, non-research pre-opening costs—such as market surveys, legal and accounting fees for operational setup, pre-opening advertising, and employee training incurred in investigating the creation or acquisition of, or creating, an active trade or business—must be capitalized as "start-up expenditures" under 26 U.S.C. § 195(a). Under IRC § 195(b), a taxpayer that makes a timely election (filed on IRS Form 4562, Part VI, no later than the due date of the return for the taxable year in which the active business begins) is permitted an immediate deduction of up to $5,000 in the taxable year in which the active trade or business commences, reduced dollar-for-dollar (but not below zero) by the amount by which cumulative start-up expenditures exceed $50,000. The remaining capitalized balance must be amortized ratably over a 180-month (15-year) period beginning with the month in which the active trade or business commences. While IRC § 195(c)(1) explicitly excludes research and experimental expenditures deductible under IRC § 174 or § 174A from § 195 startup capitalization, the underlying § 162 "carrying on" standard originally obstructed early-stage ventures from accessing the R&D tax credit.
Evolution of Section 174, Section 174A, and the Enactment of Section 41(b)(4)

To prevent tax accounting rules from penalizing early-stage research and to equalize tax treatment between established corporations with internal research divisions and pioneering startups, Congress originally enacted IRC § 174 as part of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. Rather than using the restrictive "in carrying on" phrasing of IRC § 162(a), Congress allowed taxpayers under IRC § 174(a)(1) to treat research or experimental (R&E) expenditures paid or incurred "in connection with" a trade or business as currently deductible expenses (or, under prior § 174(b), to elect to defer and amortize them over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from the expenditures).

While the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA, Pub. L. 115-97) did eliminate immediate expensing for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021—requiring taxpayers from 2022 through 2024 to capitalize and amortize specified research or experimental expenditures over five years for domestic research and 15 years for foreign research—that rule is no longer current law for domestic expenditures. On July 4, 2025, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21) enacted 26 U.S.C. § 174A, which restores immediate expensing (or an elective capitalization and ratable amortization period chosen by the taxpayer of not less than 60 months / five years) for domestic research or experimental expenditures (including software development) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Under the OBBBA transition rules, taxpayers that capitalized domestic R&E expenditures in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, may elect to deduct any remaining unamortized balance either entirely in their first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or ratably over that first taxable year and the subsequent taxable year. Moreover, small businesses meeting the gross receipts test of IRC § 448(c) for their first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (average annual gross receipts under $31 million) may elect to apply IRC § 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. In addition, the OBBBA removed the disposition basis-recovery restriction of IRC § 174(d) for domestic R&E expenditures under IRC § 174A (allowing immediate basis recovery upon disposition of property), whereas foreign R&E expenditures remain subject to mandatory capitalization, 15-year amortization, and the § 174(d) disposition restriction under revised IRC § 174. Conforming amendments in the OBBBA also updated 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) so that "qualified research" now cross-references expenditures treated as "domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A," and updated IRC §§ 280C(c), 195, 263, and 1016(a)(14) accordingly.

When Congress first created the incremental R&D tax credit in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA '81, Pub. L. 97-34, § 221, enacted August 13, 1981, initially codified as IRC § 44F, renumbered as IRC § 30 by the Deficit Reduction Act of 1984, Pub. L. 98-369, § 474, and reenacted as IRC § 41 by the Tax Reform Act of 1986, Pub. L. 99-514, § 231), it did not adopt the broader "in connection with" standard of IRC § 174. Instead, IRC § 41(b)(1) required that qualified research expenses be paid or incurred by the taxpayer "in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer"—explicitly incorporating the strict IRC § 162 standard as confirmed by Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(1). As a result, pre-revenue startups that qualified for R&E deductions under IRC § 174 were nevertheless barred from claiming the IRC § 41 research credit.

Congress corrected this structural exclusion in the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1989 (OBRA '89), Pub. L. 101-239, Title VII, § 7110, 103 Stat. 2322–2326 (enacted December 19, 1989, effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1989), by codifying 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4). Under the heading "Trade or business requirement disregarded for in-house research expenses of certain startup ventures," the statute provides that, in the case of in-house research expenses, a taxpayer shall be treated as meeting the trade or business requirement of IRC § 41(b)(1) if, at the time such in-house research expenses are paid or incurred, the principal purpose of the taxpayer in making such expenditures is to use the results of the research in the active conduct of a future trade or business—(A) of the taxpayer, or (B) of one or more other persons who with the taxpayer are treated as a single taxpayer under IRC § 41(f)(1).

body.text: Congressional Intent and the Objective "Principal Purpose" Standard

The legislative history of OBRA '89—reflected in House Ways and Means Committee Report H.R. Rep. No. 101-247 and Conference Report H.R. Conf. Rep. No. 101-386—demonstrates that Congress enacted IRC § 41(b)(4) to eliminate the competitive disadvantage faced by emerging, research-intensive ventures relative to established corporations with existing product lines. Prior to the 1989 amendment, Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(2) ("New business") enforced a rigid distinction between expanding an existing business and commencing a new business: an established conglomerate developing a new technology could rely on its existing commercial operations to satisfy IRC § 41(b)(1), whereas a standalone biotechnology, semiconductor, or software startup developing its very first product was barred from claiming the credit because expenses paid or incurred prior to commencing a new business were not considered paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business.

However, satisfying the "principal purpose" test of IRC § 41(b)(4) requires an objective demonstration at the time the expenses are paid or incurred that the taxpayer intends and is capable of using the research results in the active conduct of a future trade or business of its own (or of a controlled group or commonly controlled trade or business aggregated as a single taxpayer under IRC § 41(f)(1)). Passive investment syndicates or entities formed solely to sell, assign, or license resulting patents for royalties without actively conducting a trade or business do not satisfy the statutory mandate.
Scope of the Section 41(b)(4) Waiver: In-House vs. Contract Research Expenses

A critical statutory boundary of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4) is that its waiver of the "carrying on a trade or business" requirement applies exclusively to "in-house research expenses". Under IRC § 41(b)(1), total Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) are divided into two mutually exclusive categories: (A) in-house research expenses, and (B) contract research expenses. Because IRC § 41(b)(4) explicitly begins with the limiting phrase "In the case of in-house research expenses," contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3) remain bound by the general rule of IRC § 41(b)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(1)–(2), which require the taxpayer to be actively carrying on the particular trade or business to which the contract research relates at the time the expense is paid or incurred.
The Three Categories of In-House Research Expenses (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A))

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A) and Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b), in-house research expenses eligible for the § 41(b)(4) startup waiver are strictly restricted to three statutory categories: employee wages for qualified services, supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, and payments for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research. Any other expenditure paid or incurred in-house—such as depreciation, overhead, employee fringe benefits, travel and entertainment, or general and administrative (G&A) expenses—is excluded from in-house research expenses regardless of how the taxpayer treats those costs for financial accounting purposes or whether they are deductible under IRC § 174A.

First, under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and (D), eligible in-house wages include any wages (as defined in IRC § 3401(a) for employees, or earned income as defined in IRC § 401(c)(2) for self-employed individuals and owner-employees within the meaning of IRC § 401(c)(1)) paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services" performed by that employee. In general, IRC § 3401(a) wages correspond to taxable compensation subject to federal income tax withholding (Form W-2, Box 1 wages), including performance bonuses and taxable stock option spreads upon exercise where the underlying services in the grant year constituted qualified research (as established in Apple Computer, Inc. v. Commissioner, 98 T.C. 232 (1992), acq., 1992-2 C.B. 1, and Sun Microsystems v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1995-69, acq., 1997-2 C.B. 1), but exclude non-taxed fringe benefits and any wages taken into account in determining the work opportunity credit under IRC § 51(a) (pursuant to IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(iii)).

Second, under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and (C), eligible supplies include any tangible property used in the conduct of qualified research other than (i) land or improvements to land, and (ii) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1)–(2), supplies are used in the conduct of qualified research only if they are used in the performance of qualified services by an employee, and expenditures that are indirect research costs or G&A expenses do not qualify. Specifically, under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(i), amounts paid or incurred for utilities such as water, electricity, and natural gas used in a building where qualified research is performed are treated as G&A expenses; however, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) provides a narrow exception allowing extraordinary utility expenditures as qualified supplies to the extent the taxpayer establishes that the special character of the qualified research required additional extraordinary utility usage (such as high-energy electricity required to operate laser or nuclear research equipment).

Third, under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii), in-house expenses include amounts paid or incurred under Treasury regulations to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research, provided the taxpayer (or any person aggregated with the taxpayer under IRC § 41(f)(1)) does not receive or accrue any amount from any other person for the right to use substantially identical personal property. While 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4) historically framed this provision around off-premises "time-sharing" computers—requiring that (1) the computer is owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, (2) the computer is located off the taxpayer's premises, and (3) the taxpayer is not the computer's primary user—in modern software, artificial intelligence, and engineering practice, this provision encompasses dedicated third-party cloud computing environments (such as leased off-premises server clusters) used directly to run developmental simulations, model training, and continuous testing environments.
Qualified Services and the 80% "Substantially All" Wage Rule

For employee wages to qualify under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), the employee must perform "qualified services" as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c). Qualified services encompass three specific functional tiers. The first tier is engaging in qualified research (§ 41(b)(2)(B)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1)), which denotes the actual hands-on conduct of qualified research, such as a software architect writing experimental algorithms or a laboratory scientist conducting bench experiments. The second tier is direct supervision (§ 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2)), defined as immediate, first-line management of qualified research (for example, a lead research engineer directly supervising laboratory experiments or code architecture tests); higher-level management to whom first-line managers report does not qualify as direct supervision, even if the higher-level executive is a qualified research scientist. The third tier is direct support (§ 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3)), which covers services in direct support of either persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research or persons directly supervising qualified research (for example, a machinist machining a part for an experimental model, a clerk compiling research data, a laboratory worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research, or a secretary typing reports describing laboratory results), whereas general administrative services—such as payroll personnel preparing salary checks for scientists, accountants accounting for research expenses, janitors performing general building cleaning, or corporate officers supervising financial or personnel matters—are excluded.

The final sentence of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B), as implemented by Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2), establishes the "Substantially All" safe harbor rule for employee wages. Generally, an employee's wages are allocated to qualified services by multiplying total wages for the taxable year by the ratio of time spent performing qualified services to total work time. However, if at least 80 percent ("substantially all") of the wages paid to or incurred for an employee during the taxable year are allocated to services meeting the requirements of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) or (ii), then 100 percent of the services performed by that employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year are treated as qualified services. For early-stage startups operating under IRC § 41(b)(4), this 80/100 rule allows technical founders and lead engineers who spend at least 80% of their working time on direct R&D or first-line technical supervision to include 100% of their W-2 wages in QREs, even if up to 20% of their time is spent on administrative or fundraising tasks. If an employee's qualified time falls below 80%, only the exact documented percentage of wages attributable to qualified services may be claimed.
Contract Research Limitations (IRC § 41(b)(3))

In contrast, "contract research expenses" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(1) are defined as 65 percent of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer in carrying on a trade or business to any person other than an employee for the performance on the taxpayer's behalf of qualified research (or services that would constitute qualified services if performed by an employee). Under IRC § 41(b)(3)(C), the statutory inclusion rate increases to 75 percent for amounts paid or incurred to a "qualified research consortium"—defined as a tax-exempt organization described in IRC § 501(c)(3) or § 501(c)(6) that is organized and operated primarily to conduct scientific research, is not a private foundation, and performs qualified research on behalf of the taxpayer and one or more unrelated taxpayers. Under IRC § 41(b)(3)(D), the inclusion rate increases to 100 percent for qualified energy research payments made to an eligible small business (averaging 500 or fewer employees in either of the two preceding calendar years and less than 50% owned by the taxpayer), an institution of higher education (as defined in IRC § 3304(f)), or a federal laboratory (as defined in 15 U.S.C. § 3703(6)). Furthermore, under IRC § 41(b)(3)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(4), any prepaid contract research amounts attributable to research conducted after the close of the taxable year are treated as paid or incurred only during the period in which the qualified research is actually conducted.

Under Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3), third-party contractor payments qualify as contract research expenses only if three cumulative regulatory conditions are met: (1) the research is performed pursuant to an agreement entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, (2) the agreement provides that the research be performed "on behalf of" the taxpayer (meaning the taxpayer has a right to the research results, though exclusive rights are not required), and (3) the agreement requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful (any payment contingent on the success of the research is excluded as a payment for a finished product or result rather than for the performance of research). Additionally, under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(1), a contract research expense is disqualified if the product or result of the research is intended to be transferred to another in return for license or royalty payments and the taxpayer does not use the product in its own trade or business. Crucially, because IRC § 41(b)(4) omits contract research expenses, a pre-revenue startup that is not yet "carrying on" an active trade or business under IRC § 41(b)(1) cannot claim third-party contractor payments under the startup venture waiver. (A narrow regulatory exception exists under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(4) only for joint ventures or partnerships where the partnership itself is not carrying on the business to which the research relates, but all partners or venturers are entitled to make independent use of the research results in their own active trades or businesses).
Federal Judicial Interpretations and Case Law Governing Startup R&D Claims

While 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4) removes the requirement that a startup currently be selling goods or services to claim in-house QREs, a substantial body of federal appellate and Tax Court jurisprudence governs the four substantive pillars of any startup R&D claim: (1) the "realistic prospect" of entering an active trade or business; (2) the qualification of supplies versus depreciable property and production inventory; (3) the Four-Part Test and substantiation of the process of experimentation; and (4) the funded research exclusion.
The Trade or Business Threshold and the "Realistic Prospect" Doctrine

The judicial foundation for startup research incentives was established by the U.S. Supreme Court in Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974) (argued April 16, 1974; decided May 13, 1974). The petitioner, Edwin A. Snow, invested $10,000 for a 4% limited partnership interest in Burns Investment Company, a limited partnership formed in 1966 to develop a special-purpose trash incinerator for consumer and industrial markets conceived by general partner Trott. During 1966, Trott devoted roughly one-third of his time to testing burner models while an outside engineering shop performed fabrication work, but the incinerator had not yet been reduced to practice as a marketable product and Burns reported zero sales (though the venture was subsequently incorporated, obtained a patent in 1970, and marketed the incinerator as Trash-Away with Snow serving as Chairman of the Board). The IRS disallowed Snow's distributive share of the partnership's 1966 net operating loss under IRC § 174(a)(1), and both the U.S. Tax Court (58 T.C. 585) and the Sixth Circuit (482 F.2d 1029 (1973)) sustained the disallowance on the ground that the partnership was not yet "carrying on" a trade or business. Granting certiorari to resolve a circuit split with Cleveland v. Commissioner, 297 F.2d 169 (4th Cir. 1961), the Supreme Court reversed in an opinion by Justice William O. Douglas (joined by all participating Justices, with Justice Stewart taking no part), holding that Congress deliberately used the broader phrase "in connection with" in IRC § 174(a)(1) rather than § 162(a)'s "carrying on" standard specifically to encourage small, pioneering, and upcoming enterprises without established research departments to invest in R&D before commercial production begins.

Subsequent decisions clarified that Snow did not eliminate the trade or business requirement entirely or authorize passive tax-shelter investments. In Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984), the U.S. Tax Court held that for IRC § 174 to apply, the taxpayer must still be engaged in a trade or business of its own at some time. Where a limited partnership raised investor funds to acquire four inventions for investment purposes, took formal assignment of title, and simultaneously executed exclusive worldwide licensing agreements relinquishing all control over manufacturing, use, and marketing for the life of the patents in exchange for passive royalties, the Tax Court held that the partnership's role was purely ministerial investment management rather than a trade or business.

Building on Green, the Ninth Circuit in Kantor v. Commissioner, 998 F.2d 1514 (9th Cir. 1993) (aff'g T.C. Memo. 1990-380), articulated the governing "realistic prospect" test, holding that a nascent enterprise claiming R&D deductions must demonstrate a "realistic prospect" of subsequently entering its own trade or business in connection with the fruits of the research if the research is successful—which requires proving both (1) an objective intent to enter the business, and (2) the capability of doing so. In Kantor, a partnership consisting of passive investors advanced $3.15 million to an independent research corporation to develop computer software attachments, but simultaneously granted the research firm an option to acquire exclusive marketing rights to the software for a nominal sum of $5,000. Because it was virtually certain that the independent research firm would exercise the $5,000 option if the $3.15 million research succeeded, the Ninth Circuit held that the partnership effectively relinquished any realistic prospect of conducting a business with the research results and functioned merely as a passive investment vehicle. The Tax Court reached a parallel result in Glassley v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1996-206 (1996) (and companion jojoba syndicate decisions such as Utah Jojoba I Research v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1998-6, and Lopez v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-278), disallowing § 174 deductions and upholding negligence penalties against passive investors in a jojoba farming R&D syndicate who acted on promoter tax-benefit presentations and a cursory "glance" at the offering circular by their accountants without any realistic prospect of actively operating a trade or business.

Distinguishing Kantor, the Ninth Circuit in Scoggins v. Commissioner, 46 F.3d 950 (9th Cir. 1995) (decided February 1, 1995, rev'g T.C. Memo. 1991-263), ruled in favor of two experienced semiconductor inventors and businessmen (William V. Scoggins and Robert W. Christensen) who had designed, manufactured, and operated epitaxial reactors since 1972. After a three-year non-compete from a prior $3 million business sale expired, Scoggins and Christensen formed B & B Research and Development Partnership as sole general partners and contracted with Epitaxy Systems, Inc.—a corporation in which they owned 75% of the stock—to perform up to $500,000 of R&D ($290,000 in 1985 and $196,000 in 1986) to develop a new "pancake-heated" epitaxial reactor for silicon wafers. Under the agreement, the partnership retained technology ownership, granted the corporation only a 15-month nonexclusive marketing license (at a 20% royalty), retained an indefeasible right for the partnership to market the reactor during the first 18 months, and set the corporation's purchase option at a substantial $5 million hurdle (with at least $1 million in cash) rather than Kantor's nominal $5,000 fee. Reversing the Tax Court, the Ninth Circuit held that despite the partnership's lack of separate office furniture or employees during the R&D phase, the partners' deep technical expertise, daily direction of the research, and retained commercialization rights established both the objective intent and capability to exploit the reactor in an active business. For technology founders operating under IRC § 41(b)(4), Scoggins confirms that technical capability, active founder direction, and retained commercialization rights establish the requisite future trade or business intent.
Supplies vs. Depreciable Property and Ordinary Production Inventory

Because IRC § 41(b)(4) covers in-house supply expenses under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), startups building hardware prototypes or running pilot processes must navigate two major judicial boundaries governing IRC § 41(b)(2)(C).

In TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009) (decided November 12, 2009), the IRS disallowed supply QREs claimed by an automotive parts manufacturer for production molds built by third parties and used in product development and manufacturing, arguing that the molds were excluded under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) as "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation". The U.S. Tax Court ruled for the taxpayer, holding that whether property is of a character subject to depreciation under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) must be determined in the hands of the specific taxpayer claiming the credit. Because TG Missouri sold the production molds to its customers and the customers held the relevant economic interest and bore the risk of physical deterioration after the sale, the molds were not depreciable property in TG Missouri's hands and properly qualified as research supplies (provided all other IRC § 41 requirements were met). For hardware startups operating under IRC § 41(b)(4) that construct single-use prototypes consumed or destroyed during beta testing (or transferred to customers without retaining a depreciable economic interest), TG Missouri provides the governing legal framework to claim those material costs as supply QREs.

Conversely, in Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50 (March 10, 2009), aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. September 7, 2012), cert. denied (March 18, 2013), where a chemical manufacturer tested and evaluated new manufacturing processes during full-scale commercial production runs, the Tax Court and Second Circuit rejected the taxpayer's attempt to claim all raw materials consumed during those production runs as supply QREs. Emphasizing that under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) a plant production process must be treated as a separate business component from the product being produced, the courts held that raw materials and supplies that would have been purchased and used in ordinary commercial production regardless of whether any process research was performed are, at best, indirect research costs excluded under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1)–(2); only additional supply costs specifically incurred to evaluate the experimental process qualify. Startups transitioning from R&D to early commercial production runs must therefore bifurcate experimental supplies from standard production inventory.
The Four-Part Test, Process of Experimentation, and Substantiation

A startup invoking the IRC § 41(b)(4) trade or business waiver must still satisfy every element of the statutory Four-Part Test under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)–(3) and Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)–(6) separately for each discrete business component:

items: Section 174A / Section 174 Test (§ 41(d)(1)(A) & 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i)): The expenditures must qualify as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A (formerly § 174), meaning they are incurred in the experimental or laboratory sense to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a product or process, or the appropriate design of that product or process.

Technological in Nature Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(i) & 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(4)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature—meaning it is intended to eliminate technical uncertainty and the process of experimentation fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) (promulgated in T.D. 9104), a taxpayer is not required to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field, and may employ existing technologies and principles.

Business Component Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) & (d)(2)(B)): The application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business) for a qualified purpose—specifically a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality under § 41(d)(3)(A) (and not style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors under § 41(d)(3)(B)).

Process of Experimentation Test (§ 41(d)(1)(C) & 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)): "Substantially all"—defined by 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) (originally established in T.D. 8930) as 80 percent or more measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, without regard to the § 1.41-2(d)(2) wage rule—of the research activities for each business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation that identifies uncertainty, identifies one or more alternatives to eliminate that uncertainty, and systematically evaluates those alternatives through modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error.

body.text: Verification of the Seventh Circuit opinion confirms that Eustace did not involve internal-use software; rather, the taxpayers were shareholders in Applied Systems, Inc., a Subchapter S corporation that developed and sold commercial software packages to independent insurance agencies to manage ratings computations, multi-user file access, RAM optimization, and form-letter text editing. The Tax Court and Seventh Circuit denied the credit because Applied Systems' industrious commercial software enhancements and routine trial-and-error debugging did not seek to discover technological information or constitute a scientific process of experimentation testing hypotheses under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)–(C). Indeed, the taxpayers in Eustace specifically argued that internal-use software precedents should not apply to their commercial software, and the Seventh Circuit held that the core requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1) apply independently of the internal-use software exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(E). (The high threshold of innovation test for internal-use software under IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) was instead applied in cases such as United Stationers, Inc. v. United States, 163 F.3d 440 (7th Cir. 1998) and Norwest Corp. v. Commissioner, 110 T.C. 454 (1998)).

In Harper v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-57, the U.S. Tax Court actually ruled in favor of the taxpayers (Jeffrey and Katherine Harper, owners of S corporation Harper Construction Co., a design-build general contractor), denying the IRS's motion for partial summary judgment across $46,656 (2012) and $778,610 (2013) of claimed R&D credits. Rejecting four separate IRS challenges, the Tax Court held that Harper Construction's conceptual engineering and design work across 53 military, commercial, and renewable-energy construction projects satisfied the IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) business component test as new or improved processes, techniques, or inventions used in the contractor's trade or business. Conversely, it was in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023) (aff'g T.C. Memo. 2021-15), that the Seventh Circuit affirmed the complete disallowance of R&D credits claimed by shipbuilding subsidiary Corn Island Shipyard, Inc. (CIS) for designing and building 11 first-in-class vessels (represented at trial by the Apex 720 Tanker and the Detyens Dry Dock). Notably, while the Seventh Circuit corrected the Tax Court's legal reasoning by holding that direct support and direct supervision activities (including pilot model production wages) can be included in both the numerator and the denominator of the 80% "substantially all" fraction under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the court affirmed the disallowance and accuracy-related penalties because the taxpayer relied on arbitrary percentage estimates (such as estimating 87% of tanker hours based on differences from an earlier vessel and 60% of a lead engineer's nonproduction wages) rather than principled, contemporaneous records under IRC § 6001 and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d). The Seventh Circuit also explicitly rejected the "novelty heuristic" (that product novelty alone satisfies the 80% activities test) and held that the court could not apply the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) to smaller vessel subcomponents because the taxpayer presented its accounting on an all-or-nothing, vessel-wide basis.

In actuality, as documented in the IRS Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide, the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota in Research, Inc. v. United States denied the research credit because the taxpayer failed to substantiate its historical base-period research expenses under the statutory consistency requirement. Having included expenses for "special system projects" in its credit-year QREs while admitting it had incurred the exact same type of project expenses during the base period but had destroyed the relevant base-period documentation, the taxpayer violated the consistency mandate (now codified in IRC § 41(c)(5)(A), formerly § 41(c)(6)), rendering it impossible to accurately measure the incremental increase in research expenditures.

Fourth, in Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 691 F. Supp. 2d 688 (N.D. Tex. 2010), aff'd in part, vacated in part, and remanded, 757 F.3d 400 (5th Cir. 2014), the courts evaluated eight first-in-class prototype vessel projects from tax years ending March 1994 and March 1995 under the 80% "substantially all" rule and the shrinking-back rule (where Hurricane Katrina had destroyed subcomponent cost records, forcing an all-or-nothing vessel-level evaluation). The Fifth Circuit affirmed that three vessels (Mark V, Dirty Oil Barge, and Queen of New Orleans) qualified while five others (XFPB, T-AGS 60, Crew Rescue Boat, Hurley Dredge, and Penn Tugs) failed the 80% threshold, held that a preliminary IRS Revenue Agent Report regarding the Penn Tugs was not binding in a de novo refund suit, and vacated and remanded for factual findings under the consistency rule on whether four comparable base-period vessels (LSV, North Carolina Auto Ferry, Cajun Queen, and Ecuador) should be removed from base-period QREs.

Verification of the Tax Court opinion in Louw v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1971-326, 30 T.C.M. (CCH) 1421 (1971), confirms that the case—decided in 1971 by Judge Featherston for the 1966 tax year, a full decade before the 1981 enactment of the R&D tax credit—was an IRC § 174 deduction dispute in which the U.S. Tax Court ruled in favor of the taxpayer, Dutch-trained mechanical engineer Johan A. Louw. Distinguishing Koons v. Commissioner, 35 T.C. 1092 (1961), the Tax Court held that Louw's regular, continuous, and extensive work (devoting approximately 25 hours per week on evenings, weekends, and vacations over two to three years) developing a "Method and Apparatus for Saline Water Conversion" alongside his salaried engineering employment constituted the active trade or business of being an inventor, entitling him to deduct his $2,569 in patent attorney and technical research expenses under IRC § 174(a)(1) despite having generated zero revenue. Modern Tax Court decisions that actually denied IRC § 41 R&D tax credits in their entirety due to a lack of contemporaneous documentation linking employee wages to qualified experimentation include Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113.
The Funded Research Exclusion (IRC § 41(d)(4)(H))

Even where a startup conducts in-house research eligible under IRC § 41(b)(4) and satisfies the Four-Part Test, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(9) exclude from qualified research "any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)". Under Treasury Regulations 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(2) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(3), research performed under a contract or joint development agreement with a customer, strategic partner, or government agency is considered "funded"—and therefore disqualified for the researcher—unless the startup satisfies a strict two-pronged test based on the governing contract language. First, under the financial risk or payment contingency prong, entitlement to payment under the agreement must be contingent on the success of the research itself—as established in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995)—such that the researcher bears the financial risk of research failure and is obligated to remedy failed research at its own expense or forfeit or refund payment if technical benchmarks are not achieved. Second, under the substantial rights prong, the taxpayer performing the research must retain "substantial rights" in the research results; if the agreement confers exclusive rights to the research on the customer, or requires the researcher to pay the customer for the right to reuse the results of the research (beyond mere incidental knowledge or experience), the research is treated as fully funded.

Key federal decisions illustrate how courts scrutinize contract terms under this two-part framework. In Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. April 26, 2000), addressing major defense contracts, the Federal Circuit reversed the Court of Federal Claims on the "substantial rights" prong, holding that substantial research rights can be shared with a customer or the government and that the contractor's retained right to use the research results in its business without paying for that right is a "substantial right" under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d), even if the contractor's right is not exclusive and even if the government holds a nonexclusive license or commercial cost-recoupment rights (while also issuing an adverse substantial-variance ruling that underscores the necessity of factual specificity in administrative refund claims). Similarly, in Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, Tax Court Docket No. 405-17 (Order dated December 6, 2019 / served December 9, 2019), U.S. Tax Court Judge Robert Goeke granted summary judgment to an architectural design firm on five representative fixed-price contracts covering tax years 2010 and 2011, holding that the research was unfunded on both prongs: Populous bore the financial risk of having to incur additional expenses to remedy failed research without additional compensation (with clients holding contractual rights to review and approve design documents and dispute invoices), and even though clients retained ownership of the physical design documents and sole architectural copyrights in certain contracts, Populous retained copies and no contract provision prohibited Populous from reusing the underlying technological research results or required it to pay clients to do so.

Conversely, in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. May 6, 2024), the Eighth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the IRS disallowing Section 41 research credits claimed by a structural engineering firm for building design contracts across tax years ended September 2010, 2011, and 2013. Aligning with Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015) and Dynetics, Inc. & Subsidiaries v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015), and distinguishing Fairchild Industries, the Eighth Circuit held that general economic exposure to cost overruns under a fixed-price contract and standard professional service clauses (such as inspection, acceptance, quality assurance, compliance with building codes, and adherence to a general professional standard of care) do not mandate research success or make payment contingent on the successful outcome of the research itself. Verification of the Seventh Circuit decision (written by Circuit Judge Cudahy, with a concurrence by Circuit Judge Manion) confirms that United Stationers did not involve funded research or customer contracts; rather, United Stationers (the nation's largest office supplies wholesaler) claimed $156,457 in IRC § 41 credits for fiscal year 1988 after customizing a commercial software package ("DCS") across eight internal software projects (including DRRS, Central Invoice Project, Concept 90, Unilink, and inventory forecasting systems), and the Seventh Circuit disallowed the credit because the projects failed the technological discovery test, failed the process of experimentation test, and failed to qualify for the high-threshold-of-innovation exception to the internal-use software exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(E).
The State Tax Framework: California Revenue and Taxation Code Section 23609

For technology, life sciences, and engineering startups operating in California, federal eligibility under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4) directly intersects with California's state research tax credit under California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) § 23609 (governing C corporations and S corporations under the Corporation Tax Law) and R&TC § 17052.12 (governing individuals, partnerships, and LLCs classified as partnerships or disregarded entities under the Personal Income Tax Law), both claimed on Franchise Tax Board (FTB) Form 3523 (Research Credit) (or on amended returns via Form 100X or Form 540X within California's statute of limitations).
State IRC Conformity and Adoption of the Section 41(b)(4) Startup Waiver

While California historically conformed to the Internal Revenue Code as of January 1, 2015 (with selective modifications), the official 2025 Instructions for Form FTB 3523 confirm that for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, California law generally conforms to the Internal Revenue Code as of January 1, 2025, subject to continuing state-specific modifications. Crucially, R&TC §§ 23609 and 17052.12 conform to the federal definition of Qualified Research Expenses under IRC § 41(b)—including the 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4) startup venture exception. Consequently, a pre-revenue startup conducting in-house research in California with the principal purpose of using the research results in the active conduct of a future trade or business may immediately generate California R&D tax credits prior to generating commercial revenue. Additionally, as explicitly noted in the 2025 Form FTB 3523 Instructions, California never conformed to the federal TCJA (Pub. L. 115-97) mandatory five-year R&E amortization rules that applied federally from 2022 through 2024 (nor to the Energy Tax Act of 2005 "energy research consortium" rules under Pub. L. 109-58 or the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 modifications under Pub. L. 109-432), meaning California taxpayers continuously retained immediate R&E deductibility for state tax purposes.
Structural Divergences Between Federal IRC § 41 and California R&TC § 23609

Although California adopts the federal § 41(b)(4) startup waiver and the IRC § 41(d) Four-Part Test, R&TC §§ 23609 and 17052.12 impose mandatory state modifications governing geographic nexus, credit rates, calculation methods, gross receipts definitions, carryforwards, utilization caps, and intragroup credit assignments.

cells: IRC Conformity Baseline
Current Internal Revenue Code (including OBBBA Pub. L. 119-21 amendments to § 174A and § 41(d)(1)(A)).
Conforms to the IRC as of January 1, 2025, for taxable years beginning on or after Jan. 1, 2025, with state modifications.
Startup Trade or Business Waiver
IRC § 41(b)(4): Waives § 41(b)(1) active trade or business requirement for in-house QREs if principal purpose is active conduct of a future trade or business.
Full Conformity: Adopts IRC § 41(b)(4) for California in-house research expenses.
Geographic Nexus Mandate
Research must be conducted within the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any U.S. possession (§ 41(d)(4)(F)).
Both qualified research and basic research must be physically conducted exclusively within California.
Regular Credit Rate
20% of excess QREs over the statutory base amount (§ 41(a)(1)).
15% of excess California QREs over the California base amount.
Basic Research Credit Rate
20% of basic research payments to qualified organizations over the base period amount (§ 41(a)(2) & (e)).
24% of basic research payments paid in cash under a written contract to a qualified university or scientific research organization in California (C corporations).
Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC)
14% of QREs exceeding 50% of average QREs for the 3 preceding tax years; 6% of current-year QREs if no QREs in any of the 3 preceding tax years (§ 41(c)(4)).

Adopted for tax years beginning on or after Jan. 1, 2025 (repealing the prior AIC): 3% of CA QREs exceeding 50% of average CA QREs for the 3 preceding tax years; 1.3% of current-year CA QREs if no CA QREs in any of the 3 preceding tax years.
Gross Receipts Definition (Regular Base)
Total gross receipts (reduced by returns and allowances under § 41(c)(7)).

Only gross receipts from the sale of property held primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of business delivered or shipped to a purchaser within California (R&TC §§ 23609(h)(3), 17052.12(g)(3)).
Credit Carryback & Carryforward
1-year carryback and 20-year carryforward under General Business Credit rules (IRC § 39(a)(1)).
No carryback allowed. Unused credits carry forward indefinitely until exhausted (applied after non-carryover credits under R&TC § 23036(c), and cannot offset AMT or minimum franchise tax).
Payroll Tax Offset vs. Credit Assignment
QSB Payroll Tax Offset (§ 41(h)): Up to $500,000/year for Qualified Small Businesses (<$5M gross receipts and ≤5 years of gross receipts). Non-transferable between affiliates.
No payroll tax offset. However, R&TC § 23663 permits a C corporation to irrevocably assign credits on Form FTB 3544 to an "eligible assignee" C corporation within the same combined reporting group.
Temporary Utilization Cap
Subject to IRC § 38(c) general business credit tax liability limits.

$5,000,000 annual cap on total business credit utilization (at the group level for combined reports) for taxable years beginning on or after Jan. 1, 2024, and before Jan. 1, 2027 (R&TC § 23036.4, with 5-year refundable election option on Form FTB 3870 under R&TC § 23036.5).

body.text: The 2025 California Transition: Repeal of the AIC and Adoption of the ASC

For taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, California enacted a major structural reform to R&TC §§ 23609 and 17052.12 (stemming from FTB Legislative Proposal A): it repealed the Alternative Incremental Credit (AIC)—which previously provided three tiered rates of 1.49% (for QREs between 1% and 1.5% of average gross receipts), 1.98% (for QREs between 1.5% and 2%), and 2.48% (for QREs exceeding 2%)—and adopted a modified California Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) conforming to the mechanics of IRC § 41(c)(4). As FTB Legislative Proposal A explained, the Regular Credit method required taxpayers to substantiate historical base-period records (often dating back to 1984–1988) or apply California's specialized destination-based gross receipts rules, leading to complex audits and disallowances when decades-old records were unavailable. Under the 2025 Form FTB 3523 Instructions, because the AIC is repealed and no longer available for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, taxpayers that previously elected the AIC must affirmatively elect either the Regular Credit or the new ASC by filing Form FTB 3523; a prior AIC election will not default automatically to either method. Once elected, the California ASC remains in effect for all subsequent taxable years unless revoked with the consent of the FTB.

Under the California ASC, the credit equals 3% of current-year California QREs that exceed 50% of the average California QREs for the three preceding taxable years (modifying the federal 14% rate). However, if the taxpayer has no California QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years, the California ASC rate is a flat 1.3% of current-year California QREs (modifying the federal 6% startup rate). Furthermore, the 2025 Form FTB 3523 Instructions explicitly direct that taxpayers who have no California gross receipts under R&TC § 17052.12(h) or § 23609(i) (such as pre-revenue startups or service/licensing businesses without tangible property shipped to California purchasers) should elect the ASC. For a first-year or pre-revenue startup operating under the § 41(b)(4) waiver, the 1.3% California startup ASC provides a direct calculation based solely on current-year California QREs without requiring historical base-period gross receipts calculations.
Entity-Level Taxation and the R&TC § 23663 Election to Assign Credit

California's statutory regime also diverges by entity classification for pass-through entities and combined corporate reporting groups. For partnerships and LLCs treated as partnerships, California R&D credits are allocated among partners according to their distributive shares under a written partnership agreement pursuant to R&TC § 17039(e). Under R&TC § 23803 and the 2025 Form FTB 3523 Instructions, an S corporation computes 100% of its California R&D credit on Form FTB 3523, but may claim only one-third (1/3) of that calculated credit against its 1.5% entity-level franchise tax (or 3.5% for financial S corporations) on Schedule C (Form 100S) after applying passive activity loss and credit limits, while passing through 100% of the calculated credit to its shareholders on a pro-rata basis to offset their individual California personal income tax liabilities. If a C corporation had unused R&D credit carryovers when converting to S corporation status, those C corporation carryovers are reduced to 1/3 for entity-level use by the S corporation against its 1.5% tax, the remaining 2/3 are permanently disregarded, and none of the C corporation carryover may be passed through to shareholders. Furthermore, California R&D credits cannot offset Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT), cannot reduce corporate tax below the $800 minimum franchise tax floor, and under the temporary $5,000,000 annual business credit cap (R&TC § 23036.4, effective for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2024, and before January 1, 2027), S corporations are prohibited from electing to make entity-level disallowed credits refundable on Form FTB 3870 (whereas eligible corporate and personal income tax filers may make an irrevocable election on Form FTB 3870 under R&TC § 23036.5 to claim 20% of the capped credits annually as a refundable credit over a five-year period beginning in the third taxable year after the election year, or else have their carryover period extended by the number of years disallowed).

For C corporations, R&TC § 23663 and Title 18, California Code of Regulations (CCR) §§ 23663-1 through 23663-5 allow a C corporation ("assignor") to make an irrevocable election on an original return via FTB Form 3544 (Assignment of Credit) to assign all or part of an eligible California R&D credit to a specific affiliated C corporation ("eligible assignee") within the same combined reporting group under R&TC § 25101 or § 25110. Credits cannot be assigned generically to a division or to a disregarded Single Member LLC (SMLLC, which California treats as a division of its owner), and an assignee cannot reassign an assigned credit to another affiliate. To prevent trafficking in pre-acquisition tax attributes, the assignor must complete Part A (Side 1) of Form FTB 3544 (while the assignee completes Part B, Side 2, and both jointly identify the Key Corporation name and number), track and list credits separately by the taxable year in which they were originally allowed ("vintage"), and satisfy a strict dual-date eligibility test under 18 CCR § 23663-1. Specifically, for credits earned in taxable years beginning on or after July 1, 2008, the assignee must have been a member of the assignor's combined reporting group on both (1) the last day of the first taxable year in which the credit was allowed to the assignor, and (2) the last day of the taxable year of the assignor in which the eligible credit is assigned; for credits earned in taxable years beginning before July 1, 2008, the assignee must have been a member of the assignor's combined reporting group on both June 30, 2008, and the last day of the taxable year of the assignor in which the eligible credit is assigned.

Under 18 CCR §§ 23663-1 through 23663-5, an assignment that fails to clearly identify the vintage year, credit type, credit amount, or eligible assignee—or that assigns an amount exceeding available identical credits—is treated as a "defective assignment". Once validly assigned, the credit is permanently unavailable to the assignor for either offensive monetization or defensive audit-deficiency offset purposes, and the assignee steps into the assignor's shoes subject to all original statutory limitations (including the $5,000,000 combined reporting group-level cap for 2024–2026), even though the assignee itself is not required to perform qualified research activities.
Executive and Administrative Adjudication in California: FTB and OTA

At the state level, compliance with R&TC §§ 23609 and 17052.12 is enforced during examination by the California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) and adjudicated on administrative appeal by the California Office of Tax Appeals (OTA).
Franchise Tax Board (FTB) Audit Standards for Section 41(b)(4) Startups

In enforcing Form FTB 3523 claims, the FTB places the affirmative burden of proof squarely on the taxpayer to substantiate both the technical eligibility of every business component under the IRC § 41(d) Four-Part Test and the exact numerical accounting of California QREs. In early-stage startups operating under IRC § 41(b)(4), founders, Chief Technology Officers, and lead architects frequently divide their working hours between hands-on software or hardware engineering (qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)) and non-qualified activities such as venture capital fundraising, investor relations, market strategy, and general corporate administration. FTB audit guidelines strictly reject reliance on job titles, general job descriptions, or high-level percentage estimates unsupported by contemporaneous working papers; unless an employee clears the 80% "substantially all" threshold of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) through verifiable records, the startup must substantiate the exact chronological allocation of qualified hours using payroll records, performance evaluations, calendars and appointment books, contemporaneous project-tracking logs, version-control commits, and engineering schematics linked directly to the Four-Part Test.

Similarly, because R&TC §§ 23609 and 17052.12 restrict QREs strictly to research physically conducted within California, startups with distributed or hybrid engineering teams must track employee physical work locations and exclude wages paid to engineers working outside California—even if the startup is headquartered in California and all source code or intellectual property is centrally managed in California. For contract research expenses (claimed at 65%, or 75% for qualified research consortia, by businesses carrying on an active trade or business), the third-party vendor must physically perform the research in California.
Office of Tax Appeals (OTA) Structure and Jurisprudence

When a startup and the FTB cannot resolve an R&D credit disallowance at the audit or protest level, administrative appeals are heard by the California Office of Tax Appeals (OTA). Enacted by the Taxpayer Transparency and Fairness Act of 2017 (Assembly Bill 102, passed June 15, 2017, and signed into law by Governor Jerry Brown on June 27, 2017, and subsequently clarified by Assembly Bill 131, codified at California Government Code §§ 15670, 15674 et seq.), the legislation stripped the elected five-member State Board of Equalization (SBE/BOE) of its non-constitutional statutory duties—shifting sales, use, and excise tax administration to the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA) and transferring all administrative income, franchise, and business tax appeals jurisdiction to the independent OTA effective January 1, 2018.

Located in Sacramento and headed by a Governor-appointed, Senate-confirmed director, the OTA assigns each appeal to a panel of three Administrative Law Judges (ALJs), each of whom must be an active member of the State Bar of California for at least five years preceding appointment, possess knowledge and experience in federal and California tax laws, and subscribe to the California Supreme Court's Code of Judicial Ethics. The OTA must publish a written precedential or non-precedential opinion within 100 days after a panel's decision becomes final (after which an aggrieved taxpayer may seek a trial de novo in California Superior Court). OTA jurisprudence—exemplified by In the Matter of the Appeal of: D. Bernstein and K. Bernstein, 2025-OTA-313 (OTA Case No. 21068042, original opinion issued June 4, 2024; opinion denying petition for rehearing issued April 2, 2025)—strictly applies federal appellate precedent (including Trinity Industries II, 757 F.3d 400, Little Sandy Coal, 62 F.4th 287, Suder, and Union Carbide, 697 F.3d 104) to California R&D credit disputes. In Bernstein, a three-member OTA panel rejected the appellants' argument that performing "standard engineering" (through Processes Unlimited International, Inc.) automatically constitutes elements of a process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), held that federal IRS acceptance or summary data does not satisfy California's evidentiary burden, denied credits for a project (Kuwait 120 MBOPD Project #3748) where the Master Services Agreement showed the project commenced in March 2008 after the 2007 claim year, and reaffirmed that taxpayers must provide detailed, contemporaneous evidence enabling the panel to calculate the 80% "substantially all" fraction under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) for each business component (or subcomponent under the shrinking-back rule) conducted within California.
Hypothetical Worked Example: Federal IRC § 41(b)(4) and California R&TC § 23609 Calculation
Hypothetical Fact Pattern (NovaTech AI — Tax Year 2025)

Assume NovaTech AI is a hypothetical pre-revenue C corporation founded in January 2025, incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in Carlsbad, California. During 2025, NovaTech AI is developing a proprietary, machine-learning-driven algorithmic platform to optimize continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) data pipelines. The company has zero gross receipts, no prior operational history (no QREs in 2022, 2023, or 2024), and is funded entirely by a $4,000,000 seed venture capital equity financing (not a research grant or customer contract).

During the 2025 taxable year, NovaTech AI pays or incurs four specific categories of expenditures totaling $1,250,000: (1) $800,000 in W-2 wages paid to four backend software engineers who perform 100% qualified direct research services physically at the Carlsbad, California office; (2) $200,000 in W-2 wages paid to one remote software engineer who performs 100% qualified direct research services physically from Seattle, Washington; (3) $100,000 paid to a third-party cloud provider for dedicated off-premises testing server instances (physically located in a California data center and directed by the Carlsbad engineering team) used exclusively to run high-concurrency ingestion-layer experiments; and (4) $150,000 in legal entity formation fees and general market-research studies.
Step-by-Step Federal Calculation (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4) & § 41(c)(4)(B))

items: Application of the Section 41(b)(4) Waiver: Because NovaTech AI has no commercial product and zero sales in 2025, it is not "carrying on" an active trade or business under IRC § 162(a) or § 41(b)(1). However, because its principal purpose at the time the expenses are incurred is to actively conduct a future software business using the CI/CD platform, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4) waives the trade or business requirement for its in-house research expenses.

Determination of Federal In-House QREs: Both the $800,000 paid to the Carlsbad, California engineers and the $200,000 paid to the Seattle, Washington engineer qualify as in-house wage QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) because IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) permits research conducted anywhere within the United States ($800,000 + $200,000 = $1,000,000 in total federal wage QREs). The $100,000 paid for dedicated cloud testing servers used directly in qualified experimentation qualifies as an in-house computer lease expense under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii). Conversely, the $150,000 in legal entity formation and market-research costs is strictly excluded from QREs under IRC §§ 41(b)(2) and 41(d)(4)(D) (and must instead be capitalized/amortized under IRC §§ 195 and 248). Summing the eligible components yields Total 2025 Federal QREs of $1,100,000 ($1,000,000 + $100,000).

Federal Startup ASC Calculation (§ 41(c)(4)(B)): Because NovaTech AI had no QREs in any of the three preceding taxable years (2022–2024), its federal Alternative Simplified Credit rate under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(B)(ii) is 6% of current-year QREs, generating a Federal R&D Tax Credit of $66,000 ($1,100,000 × 6%).

Monetization via QSB Payroll Tax Offset (§ 41(h)): Because NovaTech AI has less than $5,000,000 in gross receipts for 2025 and no gross receipts for any taxable year preceding the 5-taxable-year period ending with 2025, it qualifies as a "Qualified Small Business" (QSB) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(h)(3) and may elect on IRS Form 6765 (and Form 8974) to apply the entire $66,000 credit against its federal employer payroll tax liabilities (well within the $500,000 annual cap applicable to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022, under IRC § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)(II)). Additionally, under newly enacted 26 U.S.C. § 174A, NovaTech AI may immediately deduct its domestic R&E expenditures on its 2025 federal return (subject to IRC § 280C(c) credit-reduction coordination).

body.text: Step-by-Step California Calculation (R&TC § 23609 & 2025 Form FTB 3523)

items: Determination of California In-House QREs: For California purposes, only the $800,000 paid to the four Carlsbad, California engineers qualifies as wage QREs; the $200,000 paid to the remote engineer in Seattle, Washington is completely excluded because R&TC § 23609 restricts qualified research to research physically conducted in California. The $100,000 paid for dedicated cloud testing servers located in California and used for California-based research qualifies as a California in-house research expense, while the $150,000 in legal formation and market-research costs remains excluded. Summing the eligible California components yields Total 2025 California QREs of $900,000 ($800,000 + $100,000).

California Startup ASC Calculation (R&TC § 23609): Because NovaTech AI is a 2025 startup with zero California gross receipts and no California QREs in any of the three preceding taxable years, it elects the newly adopted California ASC on Form FTB 3523 at the 1.3% startup rate, generating a California R&D Tax Credit of $11,700 ($900,000 × 1.3%).

Carryforward and Combined Benefit: Because California does not offer a payroll tax offset for QSBs, NovaTech AI carries the $11,700 California credit forward indefinitely until it generates California franchise tax liability above the $800 minimum tax (or, if part of a combined reporting group, assigns it to an eligible affiliate under R&TC § 23663). Combined federal and California credits generated in 2025 total $77,700 ($66,000 + $11,700).

body.text: Technical Substantiation and Specialist Representation

Generalist accounting practices frequently under-identify qualifying technical uncertainties in complex engineering environments—such as distributed system architectures, scalable extract-transform-load (ETL) pipelines, and real-time stream-processing analytics—or rely on high-level post-hoc wage estimates that fail IRS and FTB audit standards under Little Sandy Coal and Appeal of Bernstein.

Specifically, TaxTrex—an AI-driven R&D tax credit software platform developed from academic research published in The Tax Adviser (July 2016) on the R&D claim documentation process—uses a real-time, prospective three-survey methodology and direct accounting software integration to automate the identification and allocation of QREs while generating contemporaneous, audit-ready technical narratives mapped directly to each element of the statutory Four-Part Test (initial knowledge baseline, technological discovery, business component identification, technical uncertainty, alternatives considered, systematic evaluation methodology, and activity-expense nexus) to substantiate IRS Form 6765 (including business component reporting under Section G) and FTB Form 3523. Complementing this documentation engine, creditARMOR operates as an AI-assisted risk management, mock-audit simulation, and audit defense platform structured to evaluate project evidence across eleven documentary categories, generate draft Information Document Request (IDR) responses, score audit readiness, and mitigate IRS and FTB audit exposure (including covering defense expenses such as CPA, tax attorney, and specialist consultant fees) for early-stage startups and established enterprises claiming research credits.
